text: T-SQL for Database Administrators built a troubleshooting toolkit -- scripts a DBA keeps handy for when something's already wrong. This lesson takes that same instinct, your own scripts, no vendor required, and turns it into something that runs continuously in the background instead of only when someone's on fire. It's the free alternative to Lesson 45's commercial category -- less polished, but built entirely from things this chapter has already covered, and something you fully understand because you wrote it.

The pattern is a permanent logging table plus a procedure that fills it. dba dot PerfLog stores an identity key, a captured-at timestamp, a metric name, and a metric value. dba dot CapturePerfSnapshot inserts one row per counter straight out of sys dot dm_os_performance_counters, filtered down to the Buffer Manager and SQL Statistics objects -- the same Page Life Expectancy and batch-requests-per-second metrics this chapter has already been watching by hand.

A SQL Server Agent job with a single T-SQL step -- EXEC dba dot CapturePerfSnapshot -- scheduled to recur every fifteen minutes turns this into exactly the kind of continuous collection Lesson 45 described commercial tools providing, minus the dashboard and the invoice. Every run adds one more set of rows to the history table, which is precisely the raw material a baseline comparison, or Lesson 44's alerting job, needs to work against.

A table that only ever grows eventually becomes its own performance problem, so retention matters just as much as capture. A second job step deletes rows older than sixty days -- DELETE FROM dba dot PerfLog where CapturedAt is older than sixty days back from right now. Sixty days is long enough to compare this Monday against several previous Mondays, short enough that the table doesn't grow without bound.

A logging table sitting untouched is no better than the raw DMVs it snapshots. The real payoff is querying it deliberately -- a weekly review comparing this week's numbers against the trailing average. A table, a procedure, an Agent job, and a habit of actually looking at it gets most of a commercial tool's practical value, built from parts this course already covered.
